articles.title: Targeting the Skin Microbiome in Dermatology: Translational Hype or Emerging Therapeutic Modality?
articles.abstract: The human skin microbiome is a complex network of microorganisms, including bacteria, fungi, viruses, and archaea, that exist in a mutualistic relationship with the host. These microorganisms play important roles in maintaining skin homeostasis, defense against pathogens, regulation of immune response, and antimicrobial peptide synthesis. Dysbiosis, defined as an imbalance of microbial communities, has been linked to dermatological conditions including atopic dermatitis (AD), acne, psoriasis, and chronic wounds. Despite compelling mechanistic insights, the translation of microbiome science into clinically effective therapies remains inconsistent and prematurely optimistic. Emerging therapeutic strategies aim to restore and modulate the skin microbiome with precision, thereby moving beyond conventional broad-spectrum antimicrobial approaches. These encompass probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, live biotherapeutic products (LBPs), bacteriophage therapy, microbiome engineering, postbiotics, microbial consortia treatment, and antimicrobial peptides that selectively target microbial communities instead of eliminating them. While these strategies are biologically plausible and have initial-phase evidence, their clinical stability, reproducibility, and scalability are uncertain. Major limitations include inter-individual variability of microbiomes, transient colonization, methodological limitations in functional profiling, and regulatory uncertainties surrounding them. This review article critically evaluates microbiome-directed dermatologic therapies at the crossroads of real therapeutic potential and translational overextension. The field is not just hype; its clinical application has advanced more rapidly than the supporting evidence base justifies. Progress in this domain requires a shift from descriptive and associative research toward mechanism-driven, precision-based interventions. Such interventions must be validated against robust clinical endpoints. By critically assessing biological plausibility, clinical evidence, and translational barriers, this review provides a balanced perspective on the field and outlines realistic pathways for its evolution into a viable therapeutic paradigm.

articles.title: Allobaculum stercoricanis and Its Postbiotics Alleviate Dextran Sulfate Sodium (DSS)-Induced Colitis through the Regulation of theTLR4/NF-κB Signaling Pathway.
articles.abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a chronic intestinal disorder that has become a global public health concern. Postbiotics offer advantages in biosafety and reproducibility over probiotics. Here, we demonstrated that live Allobaculum stercoricanis (A. stercoricanis) and its two postbiotic preparations─inactivated bacterial cells (POST) and cell-free fermentation supernatant (CFS)─effectively alleviated dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis in mice. Integrated gut microbiome and serum metabolomics analyses indicated that these interventions may act through modulating bile acid metabolism and Toll-like receptor signaling pathways. Further investigations combining postbiotic metabolomics, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations identified α-muricholic acid (α-MCA) as a candidate functional metabolite, with the farnesoid X receptor (FXR) as a potential target. We hypothesize that α-MCA may contribute to ameliorating intestinal inflammation through engagement of FXR and suppression of the TLR4/NF-κB signaling pathway. These findings provide new insights into postbiotic-based therapeutic strategies for IBD.

articles.title: Beyond live probiotics: bioactivities, mechanisms, and application perspectives of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus cell-free supernatants.
articles.abstract: Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus is one of the most widely investigated probiotic species. Live preparations can modulate intestinal microbiota, support immune function, and ameliorate metabolic disorders. However, poor stability during processing and storage, low gastrointestinal survival, variable intestinal colonization, and potential risks in immunocompromised individuals limit the use of live preparations. Therefore, an increasing number of studies have focused on cell-free supernatant (CFS). Studies directly investigating CFS form the primary evidence base of this review. Findings from studies involving live cells, isolated components, mixed preparations, or other postbiotic materials are included only to provide preparation-specific mechanistic context. This review summarizes the active ingredients of CFS and the existing evidence regarding its antibacterial, antifungal, antibiofilm, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, antioxidant, antitumor, and metabolic effects. Their underlying mechanisms will be elaborated in detail, including membrane disruption, quorum-sensing interference, modulation of nuclear factor kappa B and nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 signaling, reinforcement of epithelial barrier function, as well as regulation of gut-brain and gut-liver axes. CFS offer potentially greater stability and a lower risk of microbial translocation, supporting applications in food preservation, skin care, reproductive health, metabolic intervention, and veterinary products. Future work should combine activity-guided fractionation with metabolomics, proteomics, and standardized cross-strain evaluation, while defining formulation, dose, stability, and safety requirements. These advances are essential for developing reproducible natural antimicrobial agents and functional foods based on L. rhamnosus CFS.

articles.title: Barrier Protection, Skin Microbiome, and Diaper Dermatitis in Infants: Current Evidence and Future Perspectives-A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Diaper dermatitis is one of the most common inflammatory skin conditions in infancy. It develops through the combined effects of moisture, friction, irritants, and disruption of the epidermal barrier. This review aimed to evaluate recent evidence on barrier-supportive ingredients used in infant diaper care, with a focus on barrier protection, microbiome-related approaches, and their role in preventing and managing diaper dermatitis. A structured literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science identified clinical studies involving infants and young children of diaper-wearing age that evaluated diaper-area interventions or implementation strategies and reported diaper dermatitis or related skin outcomes, including erythema, transepidermal water loss, skin pH, and hydration. The final clinical evidence synthesis included 35 independent studies reported in 34 publications. Reviews and relevant experimental or mechanistic studies were used to provide background and biological context but were not considered direct evidence of clinical efficacy in infants. Clinical findings were synthesized narratively according to intervention type, study design, population, outcomes, and key limitations. Direct clinical evidence supports barrier-protective care, appropriate cleansing practices, and diaper-related strategies as core components of diaper dermatitis prevention and management, although findings varied by formulation, population, and outcome. Evidence for botanical and natural topical interventions was formulation-specific and inconsistent across studies. Microbiome-targeted approaches, including postbiotics, are biologically plausible and supported primarily by experimental and mechanistic evidence; however, direct clinical evidence in infant diaper dermatitis remains limited.

articles.title: Microbiome-Derived Metabolic Signaling in the Gut-Skin Axis: Implications for Nutricosmetics and Healthy Skin Aging.
articles.abstract: The gut-skin axis represents a bidirectional communication network linking the gut microbiota, microbial metabolism, immune regulation, and skin physiology. Natural bioactives derived from dietary plants, mushrooms, fermented foods, marine resources, and functional ingredients may influence skin health through both direct nutritional effects and host-microbiome metabolic interactions. This review provides a microbiome-centered, systems-level perspective on the relationships among dietary bioactives, gut microbial biotransformation, microbiome-derived metabolites, and skin aging-associated physiology. Particular attention is given to polyphenols, polysaccharides, carotenoids, peptides, fatty acids, probiotics, postbiotics, and fermented bioactive compounds as modulators of microbial composition and metabolic activity. Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), indole derivatives, urolithins, phenolic metabolites, bile acid derivatives, and lipid-associated metabolites, are discussed as potential mediators linking diet and microbial metabolism with skin physiology. Their relevance to oxidative stress, inflammation, mitochondrial function, epidermal barrier homeostasis, extracellular matrix remodeling, and cellular senescence is critically evaluated according to the available level of evidence. Human intervention studies provide preliminary clinical support for selected probiotic and oral nutricosmetic interventions; however, direct evidence establishing microbiome-mediated effects on skin outcomes remains limited. Interindividual differences in microbial metabolic capacity may further contribute to heterogeneous responses to dietary interventions. Overall, this evidence-centered appraisal reveals a substantial gap between mechanistic plausibility and demonstrated human causality, emphasizing the need for studies that directly test microbiome mediation using integrated microbiome, metabolite, and skin-specific outcome measurements.

articles.title: Beyond the skin barrier: nanocarrier-based drug delivery with emerging insights into the gut-skin axis and probiotic modulation in atopic dermatitis.
articles.abstract: To summarize recent advances in nanotechnology-based topical drug delivery systems for atopic dermatitis (AD) and highlight their potential to overcome the limitations of conventional topical therapies, particularly poor skin penetration, adverse effects, and inadequate drug concentrations in deeper skin layers.

articles.title: Research advances on postbiotics in promoting skin wound healing: mechanisms, formulations, and clinical translation.
articles.abstract: Wound healing is a complex process involving different cell types, molecules and stages in the dermis, epidermis and associated microbiome. Chronic wounds caused by pressure, diabetes, or immunodeficiency often have huge economic and therapeutic costs. Postbiotics, in particular inactivated bacteria, cell components and metabolites, are emerging as novel treatments targeting the skin microbiome and provide precise treatment options for wound healing, inflammation, angiogenesis and re-epithelialization. articles.title: From fruit waste to foods via fermentation.
articles.abstract: The increasing generation of fruit waste represents a major environmental and economic challenge for the agri-food sector, while also offering significant opportunities for sustainable valorisation within the framework of the circular economy. Fruits rejected for cosmetic reasons, together with processing by-products, are rich sources of dietary fibre, sugars and bioactive compounds that can be converted into value-added products. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of microbial fermentation as a sustainable strategy for fruit waste valorisation, with particular emphasis on the role of lactic acid bacteria, acetic acid bacteria, yeasts and microbial consortia in improving the nutritional, technological and functional properties of fruit-derived substrates. Current evidence demonstrates that microbial fermentation not only preserves fruit biomass but also enhances its value through the degradation of complex carbohydrates, the biotransformation of phenolic compounds, the production of bioactive metabolites and the generation of functional ingredients. This review further discusses the contribution of viable microorganisms and postbiotic components to product functionality, as well as the importance of microbial viability, processing conditions and storage stability for the development of safe and functional fermented foods. In addition, it highlights recent advances in the use of microbial consortia and identifies the mechanisms governing microorganism-plant matrix interactions as a key area requiring further investigation. Overall, the available literature supports fermentation as a versatile and effective strategy for transforming fruit waste into high-value food products. By integrating current knowledge on microbial metabolism, functionality and processing challenges, this review identifies the main scientific and technological gaps and outlines future research priorities, including microbial consortium design, process scale-up, regulatory considerations and life cycle assessment, to facilitate the industrial implementation of sustainable fruit waste biorefineries.

articles.title: Hypoxia-Induced Gut-Brain Axis Remodeling and Insomnia: Mechanisms and Microbiota Adaptive Regulation from a Translational Perspective.
articles.abstract: High-altitude hypoxia frequently disrupts sleep-wake cycles, causing insomnia that impairs acclimatization, performance, and health. Emerging evidence implicates the gut-brain axis (GBA) in this disorder. Prolonged or severe hypoxia can disturb intestinal epithelial homeostasis through oxidative, inflammatory, and metabolic changes, increasing barrier permeability and facilitating the translocation of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and other bacterial products into the circulation. Concurrent gut microbial dysbiosis reduces the production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and redirects tryptophan metabolism toward the kynurenine pathway, thereby promoting systemic and neuroinflammation. Peripheral inflammatory signals communicate with the central nervous system (CNS) through a compromised blood-brain barrier (BBB), circumventricular organs (CVOs), and vagal afferents, while neuroendocrine stress responses involving the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and cortisol may further link hypoxia and inflammation to sleep disruption. Together, these pathways activate arousal circuits while inhibiting sleep-promoting gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-ergic neurons, contributing to the characteristic electroencephalographic features of high-altitude insomnia. High-altitude-specific evidence for conventional sleep therapies remains limited, underscoring the need for biologically grounded strategies tailored to hypoxic environments. Preliminary probiotic evidence suggests potential benefits for oxygenation and acclimatization, whereas postbiotics and dietary pre-habilitation represent mechanistically promising approaches. However, the absence of human randomized controlled trials using polysomnography remains a major translational barrier. Future research should prioritize field-deployable diagnostic tools, causal multi-omics studies, and personalized microbiota-targeted interventions for high-altitude insomnia.
